Video Game Genre. Video game genre is the classification system for games based on gameplay mechanics, player objectives, and experiential focus. Like film genres such as westerns and comedies, game genres organize player expectations and define what skills, strategies, and emotional responses a game will demand. Understanding genre is essential to understanding game culture, esports, and how games evolved as a medium.

First-person shooter games prioritize combat, rapid reflexes, and aiming. They define a large portion of esports and gaming culture. Counter-Strike, Call of Duty, and Halo are genre-defining titles that established the competitive standard for the medium.

Role-playing games emphasize character progression, dialogue, narrative choice, and statistical systems inherited from tabletop games. They can be single-player epics like Skyrim or massive multiplayer worlds spanning years of play.

Strategy games, turn-based or real-time, require resource management, long-term planning, and tactical thinking. They range from competitive esports titles like StarCraft to board-game adaptations that challenge players intellectually.

Action-adventure games blend exploration, combat, puzzle-solving, and narrative. They are often single-player focused and emphasize immersion and cinematic presentation, creating seamless worlds.

Board game adaptations in digital form translate physical game mechanics into digital spaces, preserving core rules while adding convenience and reaching new audiences.

Genre boundaries are porous. Games often blend genres such as action-role-playing games and tactical shooters. Genre conventions shift as technology and player expectations evolve over time.

Esports have formalized certain genres including first-person shooters, multiplayer online battle arenas, and strategy games as competitive disciplines. Genre choice affects whether a game can support competitive play at professional levels.
